name: CRDTs & Conflict-Free Replicated Data
tagline: Join-semilattice data structures whose concurrent updates commute, guaranteeing Strong Eventual Consistency without consensus round-trips.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of CRDTs—from CvRDT join-semilattices and OR-Sets to HLC clock hygiene, tombstone compaction, and delta-CRDTs.

spark.summary: CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are replicated data structures whose concurrent updates commute or form a mathematical join-semilattice, guaranteeing every replica converges to the exact same state without coordination or consensus.
spark.keyTakeaway: CRDTs eliminate consensus round-trips for local-first apps and geo-distributed active-active stores by trading coordination latency for metadata overhead (vector clocks, tombstones, or per-element IDs).
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Traditional replication relies on consensus (Raft/Paxos) to agree on a global total order of writes.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Active-Active CRDT Gossip & Semilattice Merge (Replica Mumbai -> Replica Frankfurt -> Replica Virginia -> Converged State); Concurrent Remove & Re-Add Across Partitioned Replicas (Replica R1 -> Async Gossip -> Replica R2); CRDT Element & Causal Compaction State Machine (LIVE ELEMENT -> TOMBSTONED -> COMPACTED).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choose between shipping full state, causal operations, or compact deltas depending on network reliability and object size. In production, CRDTs move through active writes, delta replication, and causal-barrier compaction.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Compare CRDTs against Raft consensus, multi-master split-brain recovery, and PACELC consistency-latency trade-offs.

learningJourney.title: What are CRDTs (Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types)
learningJourney.explanation:
Traditional replication relies on consensus (Raft/Paxos) to agree on a global total order of writes. **CRDTs** invert the problem: instead of agreeing on *when* operations happened, design the data structure so *order does not matter*.

A state-based CRDT (**CvRDT**) forms a **bounded join-semilattice** `(S, ⊔)` whose merge operator `⊔` is **associative**, **commutative**, and **idempotent** (`A ⊔ A = A`). Any two replicas receiving the same updates—in any order, with any duplicates—mathematically converge to **Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC)**.

sectionDiagram.title: Active-Active CRDT Gossip & Semilattice Merge
sectionDiagram.summary: Every replica accepts local writes at 0 ms and converges deterministically via associative, commutative, idempotent merges.

learningJourney.title: Why we need CRDTs (and How OR-Sets Prevent Lost Re-Adds)
learningJourney.explanation: Consensus protocols require 50–150 ms WAN quorum round-trips and stall during network partitions. Collaborative editors (Yjs, Automerge) and active-active carts need 0 ms local writes—even offline. In an **Observed-Remove Set (OR-Set)**, tagging each addition with a unique `(replicaId, seq)` ensures a concurrent `remove()` only tombstones the specific tags it *observed*, preserving concurrent re-adds.

sectionDiagram.summary: Tagging every add with a unique ID ensures R1's stale remove cannot erase R2's concurrent re-add.

comparison.choice: Use: Local-First Editors, Carts, Counters & Presence
benefits: 0 ms local write latency, offline-first operation, 100% AP availability under partitions.
costs: Metadata overhead (vector clocks, tombstones, per-char IDs).

comparison.choice: Avoid: Negative Bank Balances & Unique Usernames
benefits: Use Raft/Paxos consensus or single-leader serialization for strict global invariants.
costs: Two replicas concurrently decrementing a `PN-Counter` from 1 can drive it to -1.

comparison.choice: Avoid: High-Churn Delete Sets Without Epoch GC
benefits: Run causal-barrier compaction or epoch snapshots before tombstones OOM.
costs: Aggressive tombstone pruning before offline clients sync causes zombie resurrection.

learningJourney.title: How to manage Replica IDs, HLCs & Tombstone Compaction
learningJourney.explanation:
1. **Unique `replicaId`**: Generate a cryptographically random 64/128-bit `clientId` per tab/instance—never reuse `userId` or hostnames.
2. **Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)**: Never use raw `Date.now()` in LWW-Registers; an NTP-skewed client will silently overwrite all newer edits.
3. **Run-Length Encoding & Causal GC**: Production engines like Yjs (`Item` structs) and Automerge 2.0 (columnar change logs) RLE-compress contiguous character IDs and compact tombstones only below the minimum causal frontier of active replicas.

benefits: Tolerates dropped, duplicated, and reordered packets over plain HTTP/gossip.
costs: Bandwidth scales as O(full state size) on every sync.
Requires reliable causal broadcast—cannot drop or reorder causal dependencies.

benefits: Ships small idempotent state fragments; combines tiny payloads with loss-tolerant gossip.
costs: Requires tracking anti-entropy delta intervals per peer.

learningJourney.explanation: In production, CRDTs move through active writes, delta replication, and causal-barrier compaction. Never purge tombstones until all active replicas acknowledge the causal version vector—and force stale offline clients (>30 days) to re-bootstrap from a fresh epoch snapshot.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does an LWW-Register CRDT using raw client `Date.now()` timestamps fail in production, and how do you fix it?

options.text: A replica with a fast-skewed NTP clock silently overwrites newer edits from other nodes; fix it with Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) + replicaId tie-breakers
options.feedback: Correct: HLCs bound physical clock skew with logical monotonic counters.
LWW-Register merge is idempotent (`max(ts1, ts2)`), but wall-clock skew breaks recency semantics.

options.text: Switching from CvRDT to CmRDT eliminates clock skew
options.feedback: LWW semantics still depend on the timestamp source regardless of state vs op transport.
